title: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
outcome: The proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is justiciable. Secularism is part of the basic structure. The Court laid down strict guidelines for the exercise of power under Article 356.
ratio: A proclamation under Article 356 is amenable to judicial review.
Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.
The power under Article 356 is exceptional and must be used sparingly; the Court can examine whether the material on which the President acted was relevant.
Floor test in the Legislative Assembly is the appropriate method to test majority support, not the subjective satisfaction of the Governor alone.

key_holdings.holding: Judicial review of Article 356 proclamations permitted
Secularism is part of the basic structure
Strict limitations on the use of President's Rule

overruled_or_modified: Significantly narrowed the scope of State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) on the justiciability of Article 356
followed_by: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
Subsequent decisions on President's Rule and federalism
summary: S.R. Bommai is the leading authority on the scope of Article 356 and the federal character of the Indian Constitution. A nine-judge bench held that proclamations of President's Rule are justiciable, that secularism is part of the basic structure, and that the power to dismiss State governments must be exercised with extreme caution.
content_for_rag:
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) 3 SCC 1 is a landmark nine-judge bench decision that redefined the contours of federalism and the use of President's Rule under Article 356 of the Constitution.

The case arose out of the dismissal of several State governments between 1989 and 1991. The principal questions before the Court were whether a proclamation under Article 356 was justiciable and what were the limitations on the President's power to impose President's Rule.

The Court held that the power under Article 356 is not absolute. A proclamation is open to judicial review on grounds of illegality, malafides, and relevance of the material on which it is based. The Court emphasised that the satisfaction of the President (based on the Governor's report) is not beyond scrutiny. It further held that the proper method to determine whether a government has lost majority is a floor test on the floor of the Legislative Assembly, not the personal opinion of the Governor.

Crucially, the Court declared that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution. A State government that acts against the constitutional principle of secularism can be legitimately dismissed under Article 356. The decision significantly curtailed the frequent and often political use of President's Rule and strengthened the federal structure of the Indian Constitution.
